Hello everyone, I’m George Fan. In the upcoming video, I will share with you my personal experiences and insights, as well as those of my company Ziyutec Inc., in Canadian federal government engineering projects.

This episode will focus on the characteristics and operational methods of federal government projects. Since 2005, I have been involved in federal government engineering projects, so I am quite familiar with the process.

Three years ago, my company started undertaking government projects. What you’re seeing now is our company’s website. Over the past two to three years, we have completed over ten projects for the Canadian federal government. The company website showcases some representative case studies, and I’ll now open the website for you to review.

Our government projects have a wide coverage, including Ontario, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba.

Our government projects have a wide coverage, including Ontario, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba.

Currently displayed are several projects located in British Columbia (BC). The first two are situated in Prince George and Surrey respectively, while another is in Manitoba.

Additionally, we have previously completed projects for the Canadian federal government in Ontario, such as the Eastern Memorial Building.

In Saskatchewan, we participated in the Income Tax Building and DDC Life Cycle Replacement projects in Regina.

In both Regina and Surrey, we have undertaken Fire Alarm Upgrading projects to provide services for two government office buildings. These are some of the cases that our company and I have participated in for Canadian federal government projects in recent years.

Federal government projects have the following characteristics.

Federal government projects have the following characteristics.

First, their advantages include:
- Guaranteed design fees
- Standardized management
- Helps enhance company reputation
- Higher fees and stable projects (due to annual budgets allocated for updates or new projects)

However, federal government projects also present certain challenges:
- Heavy documentation workload
- Large review teams and complex processes (each design phase requires extensive document submissions)
- Strict project requirements (including security clearances for both individuals and companies)
- Teams must possess strong professional backgrounds and relevant project experience

During the bidding process, most projects require proposals containing the following:
- Security clearance information
- Team qualifications
- Project plan and schedule
(where pricing accounts for only 10% of the evaluation weight)

Currently, government projects can be obtained through multiple channels.

Government projects can be obtained through multiple channels.

The first channel is through government websites. Almost all Canadian federal government programs, such as those from the Department of National Defence, are managed by a department called PSPC, which stands for Public Services and Procurement Canada.

In terms of management, the agency has a dedicated department responsible for this, called Buyandsell.gc.ca. This platform oversees the tendering, bidding, and subsequent supervision processes for projects. The related procedures are quite cumbersome, requiring the submission of numerous documents and information through a specific system. I have participated in such projects before but ultimately withdrew due to the time-consuming process and overly complex paperwork.

The platform is open to all businesses. Regarding project scale, large-scale projects typically adopt an invitation-based bidding approach, limited only to specific large enterprises rather than offering equal competition opportunities to all companies. For small and medium-sized projects, Buyandsell.gc.ca serves as a portal platform where businesses can register as qualified suppliers to participate in bidding.

Additionally, there is a more convenient way to submit bids through the BGIS Platform. The specific steps will be demonstrated in a follow-up video.

BGIS is a large property management company that has signed a ten-year Master Agreement with Public Services and Procurement Canada (PSPC), responsible for managing most small and medium-sized Capital Projects across Canada. These project details are published on the official BGIS website.

All parties can download the tender documents and submit proposals to participate in the bidding through the website www.bgismer.com.

In terms of management, once the bid is won, your direct client will be BGIS, not PWGSC.

BGIS adopts two management approaches.

The first is called Standing Offer, where qualified companies sign a Standing Offer agreement with BGIS, which may be valid for one, three, or five years. When projects arise, BGIS offers these opportunities to a limited number of companies that have signed Standing Offers, while other companies without Standing Offers cannot see these opportunities.

The second approach is open to the public, which refers to the currently published open tender projects.

The second approach is open to the public, referring to currently published open tender projects.

These opportunities include consulting projects and construction projects, covering both design and construction aspects. The specific procedures for how to apply, register, bid, and prepare tender documents will be explained in detail in subsequent videos.

Assuming we have successfully secured a project, I will briefly introduce the necessary documents required for the project.

For design projects, once a project is undertaken, it is mandatory to strictly adhere to the PSPC National CAD Standards during the drafting process. This standard system is complex and highly detailed, requiring all drawings to comply with this Computer-Aided Design and Drafting standard.

The document spans fifty to sixty pages, establishing detailed specifications for various professional fields, including layer settings, printing standards, and title block formats.

Everyone can look up these publicly available drawing standards online.

The design document also includes a standard for specification guidelines. This standard provides a template, requiring all specifications to be written in the prescribed format.

NMS was compiled by the National Research Council of Canada, with its content divided into over thirty standard categories.

For example, the mechanical section corresponds to 21, 23, and 25, while the electrical section corresponds to 26, 27, and 28. Each section further contains different chapters with detailed content.

The mechanical section corresponds to 21, 23, and 25, while the electrical section corresponds to 26, 27, and 28. Each section further contains different chapters with detailed content.

This information is publicly available. You can search for NMS on the National Research Council (NRC) of Canada website to access the relevant content.

So what is the specific process for signing the contract? Taking a design project as an example, there are usually two standard contracts to choose from.

For example, my company Ziyutec Inc. adopted the RAIC standard, which stands for The Royal Architectural Institute of Canada, in the Prince George project.

These are standard contract templates with additional clauses included. This one is the Architectural Consulting Contract. For engineering-related contracts, the version from the Association of Consulting Engineering Companies Canada (ACEC) is adopted.

This is an “ENGINEERING AGREEMENT BETWEEN CLIENT AND ENGINEER” contract. For friends engaged in construction, there is another standard contract CCDC available as an alternative.

Our company primarily provides engineering consulting services and typically does not involve contract signing. However, when participating in Canadian federal government projects, as engineering consultants, we are required to assist BGIS in construction management. For this purpose, we need to prepare CCDC contract documents. As shown in the illustration, this is the CCDC document we designed for the Prince George project.
